analysis.one_liner: Bans corporations convicted of serious crimes from funding political campaigns for ten years.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it was introduced in May 2024 and died in committee when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal campaign law to make it illegal for a corporation convicted of a serious crime — or one that paid $1 million or more to settle felony charges through a deferred or non-prosecution agreement — to spend money on any federal, state, or local election for ten years. That ban would cover direct contributions, independent spending, and political ads. Companies under such settlements would be barred from influencing elections for a decade.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters would get a say in elections unshaped by companies that have been convicted of crimes like defrauding the United States or have paid at least $1 million to resolve felony charges. Campaigns would no longer be able to draw on these corporations' treasuries, and the public would see less money from companies with recent criminal records in political advertising.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters and candidates competing for clean money

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful for any corporation convicted of conspiring to defraud the United States or of another felony involving dishonesty or breach of trust — or for its political action fund — to make campaign contributions, independent expenditures, or electioneering communications for federal, state, or local elections.

Corporations that were charged with such felonies and resolved them through deferred prosecution or non-prosecution agreements requiring payments of $1 million or more are treated the same as convicted companies.
The ban lasts ten years from the conviction or the agreement, and it applies to any corporation that is convicted or signs such an agreement after the bill becomes law.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations with recent felony convictions or large deferred-prosecution settlements would lose their ability to fund candidates and political ads for a decade, including through their political action committees. The restriction reaches spending on state and local races, not just federal ones.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations with felony convictions or major settlements

drawbacks.text: The ban covers only a narrow slice of crimes: convictions for conspiracy to defraud the United States or other felonies involving dishonesty or breach of trust, plus large deferred-prosecution agreements. A company convicted of, say, a serious environmental or workplace-safety felony outside those categories could keep spending.

The restriction might face a constitutional challenge, since Supreme Court decisions beginning with Citizens United v. FEC treat corporate political spending as protected speech; courts have upheld narrower corruption-based limits, and whether a conviction-based ban survives is untested.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is straightforward: a company found guilty of defrauding the government shouldn't spend its treasury influencing the government that convicted it, and paying $1 million or more to settle felony charges without trial shouldn't be a loophole. The cost falls on a small set of companies with criminal records, and the main honest concerns are the narrow range of crimes covered and the legal uncertainty under current First Amendment doctrine. Nothing in the bill imposes costs on ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ilhan Omar introduced the bill on May 23, 2024, joined by Reps. Schakowsky, Tlaib, and Pressley.
That same day, the House referred it to the Committee on House Administration, the panel that handles campaign finance and election law.
The committee took no further action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died there when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations with criminal convictions or large settlements keep their unrestricted right to spend on elections, and no one had to defend the practice publicly — the bill died without a hearing or a vote.

for.name: Rep. Ilhan Omar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it to the House Administration committee.

for.name: Reps. Jan Schakowsky, Rashida Tlaib, and Ayanna Pressley
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee of referral for campaign finance bills
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Rep. Bryan Steil
against.role: Chair, House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired committee to which it was referred never acted on it.

industries.industry: Corporations with felony convictions or large deferred-prosecution settlements
industries.note: The bill would strip these companies of the right to fund candidates and election ads for ten years, including through their political action committees. Their interest in the bill's defeat ran against voters' interest in elections not financed by companies with recent criminal records.
